Wickedly
WIK-ed-lee
adv.
From wicked, Middle English wikked, related to wicca, a sorcerer. Webster 1828: in a manner or with motives contrary to the divine law; viciously; corruptly. In the Authorized Version the adverb is the standing word of national confession — we have done wickedly — and of the historians’ verdict on particular kings.

Biblical Definition

Wickedly is what the penitent says about himself and what the historian says about a king. Nehemiah’s great prayer of confession states both halves of the covenant lawsuit: thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly (Nehemiah 9:33). Daniel confesses in the same terms: We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts (Daniel 9:5), and the psalmist joins himself to his fathers in it: We have sinned with our fathers, we have committed iniquity, we have done wickedly (Psalm 106:6). Notice that all three are corporate. The word also carries the verdicts. Manasseh hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did (2 Kings 21:11). Ahaziah’s mother was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:3), which is one of the saddest lines in Chronicles. Lot pleads with the men of Sodom, do not so wickedly (Genesis 19:7). And Job asks the question that keeps the word honest: Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him? (Job 13:7) — a warning that a man may sin in the very act of defending the Almighty.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WICKEDLY as in a manner or with motives and designs contrary to the divine law; viciously; corruptly; immorally. The KJV uses it above all in the great corporate confessions.

expand to see more

WICKEDLY, adv. — In a manner or with motives and designs contrary to the divine law; viciously; corruptly; immorally.

WICKED, a. — Evil in principle or practice; deviating from the divine law; addicted to vice; sinful; immoral.

Webster grounds the definition in the divine law rather than in social harm, which is the biblical footing. Wickedness is measured against a revealed standard, not against consequences.

Key Scripture

Genesis 19:7 — "And said, I pray you, brethren, do not so wickedly."

2 Kings 21:11 — "Because Manasseh king of Judah hath done these abominations, and hath done wickedly above all that the Amorites did, which were before him, and hath made Judah also to sin with his idols:"

Nehemiah 9:33 — "Howbeit thou art just in all that is brought upon us; for thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly:"

Daniel 9:5 — "We have sinned, and have committed iniquity, and have done wickedly, and have rebelled, even by departing from thy precepts and from thy judgments:"

Job 13:7 — "Will ye speak wickedly for God? and talk deceitfully for him?"

Modern Corruption

The adverb is corrupted by the therapeutic reframing of sin — wickedness described as dysfunction, damage, or unmet need — and by the disappearance of corporate confession, which every biblical instance of the word models.

expand to see more

Nehemiah 9:33, Daniel 9:5, and Psalm 106:6 all say we. Not one of the three men praying was chiefly responsible for what he confesses; Daniel in particular is among the most blameless figures in the Old Testament, and he numbers himself with the rebels without qualification or distancing. The modern instinct, in and out of the church, is the reverse: to identify the guilty party as someone else and to describe one’s own share as a product of circumstance. Where sin is renamed as damage and repentance is replaced by explanation, these prayers become unsayable. They are the church’s pattern for corporate confession and they require the plain word.

Job 13:7 guards the other flank. Job’s friends were defending God’s justice, and Job charges them with speaking wickedly for God. It is possible to sin in the act of contending for the truth — by misrepresenting God’s dealings, by accusing a sufferer to protect a theory, by talking deceitfully in a good cause. The Lord’s own verdict at the end of the book vindicates Job on this point: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right, as my servant Job hath (Job 42:7). Zeal for orthodoxy does not license careless speech about God or cruel speech about the afflicted.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew is chiefly rasha', to be wicked or guilty, and its causative to act wickedly; it is the standard covenant-lawsuit term for the party in the wrong before the judge.

expand to see more

Hebrew rasha' (H7561) — to be wicked, to act wickedly; in the covenant lawsuit, to be the guilty party (Nehemiah 9:33; Daniel 9:5; Psalm 106:6).

Hebrew ra'a' (H7489) — to do evil, to act badly; behind done wickedly above all that the Amorites did (2 Kings 21:11).

Hebrew 'avlah (H5766) — injustice, unrighteousness; speak wickedly for God in Job 13:7 is literally to speak unrighteousness for Him.

The confession formula chata'nu, he'evinu, hirsha'nu — we have sinned, committed iniquity, done wickedly — recurs across Daniel 9, Psalm 106, and 1 Kings 8.

Webster derives English wicked from a root connected with sorcery, which preserves the sense of an active, willed evil rather than a lapse.

Usage

"Thou hast done right, but we have done wickedly (Nehemiah 9:33) — the covenant lawsuit conceded; God justified and the people condemned."

"His mother was his counsellor to do wickedly (2 Chronicles 22:3) — wickedness taught inside a household."

"Will ye speak wickedly for God? (Job 13:7) — a man may sin in the act of defending the Almighty."
